vjimc-1998-cat2-01.title: Perturb the eigenvector
vjimc-1998-cat2-01.body:
The inner product is linear in the first argument. Let $x\in E^\perp$ and $\varphi\in E$. We must show $(Tx,\varphi)=0$. We may assume $\|x\|=\|\varphi\|=1$ (the claim is homogeneous; it is trivial if $x=0$ or $\varphi=0$).

**Expanding the quadratic form.** For $t\in\mathbb C$ let $\psi=\varphi+tx$. Since $(x,\varphi)=0$, we get $\|\psi\|^2=1+|t|^2$. Also $(T\varphi,x)=\mu(\varphi,x)=0$ and $(T\varphi,\varphi)=\mu$, so
$$(T\psi,\psi)=(T\varphi,\varphi)+t(Tx,\varphi)+\bar t(T\varphi,x)+|t|^2(Tx,x)=\mu+tc+|t|^2d,$$
where $c=(Tx,\varphi)$ and $d=(Tx,x)$. The hypothesis gives
$$|\mu+tc+|t|^2d|\le1+|t|^2\qquad\text{for all }t\in\mathbb C. \tag{$*$}$$

**Choosing $t$.** Suppose $c\ne0$. For $s>0$ take $t=s\,\mu\,\frac{\bar c}{|c|}$, so $|t|=s$ and $tc=s\mu|c|$. Then
$$|\mu+tc+|t|^2d|=|\mu(1+s|c|)+s^2d|\ge(1+s|c|)-s^2|d| .$$
Combining with $(*)$: $1+s|c|-s^2|d|\le1+s^2$, i.e. $|c|\le s(1+|d|)$ for every $s>0$. Letting $s\to0^+$ gives $|c|\le 0$, contradicting $c\ne0$.

Hence $(Tx,\varphi)=0$ for all $\varphi\in E$, i.e. $Tx\in E^\perp$. So $T(E^\perp)\subseteq E^\perp$. ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-02.title: Exhibit one
vjimc-1998-cat2-02.body:
**Yes.** The members are exactly the integers $m\ge1998$ with $m\equiv1998\pmod{131}$. Since $1998=15\cdot131+33$, the condition is $m\equiv33\pmod{131}$.

The palindrome $170071$ works:
$$170071-1998=168073=131\cdot1283,$$
so $170071=1998+1283\cdot131=a_{1284}$. (A computer search shows it is the smallest palindromic member.)

**Answer: Yes** (e.g. $a_{1284}=170071$). ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-02.title: A palindrome made of ones, via Fermat's little theorem
vjimc-1998-cat2-02.body:
Since $131$ is prime and $131\nmid10$, Fermat's little theorem gives $10^{130}\equiv1\pmod{131}$. Consider
$$R=\sum_{i=0}^{32}10^{130i}=1\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{129}1\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{129}1\cdots1\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{129}1 ,$$
which has $33$ digits $1$ at the positions $0,130,\dots,4160$ and zeros elsewhere. Reversing the digits maps position $p$ to $4160-p$, and $4160-p$ is a multiple of $130$ iff $p$ is, so $R$ is a palindrome.

Modulo $131$, every term $10^{130i}\equiv1$, so $R\equiv33\equiv1998\pmod{131}$. Since $R>1998$, $R=1998+131m$ for some integer $m\ge1$, i.e. $R=a_{m+1}$ is a member of the progression.

The same idea works for any progression whose difference is coprime to $10$ (use $\varphi(d)$ in place of $130$). ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-03.title: Multiply by $1-z$ and use the triangle inequality
vjimc-1998-cat2-03.body:
If $n=0$, $P=a_0\ne0$ has no roots. Let $n\ge1$ and $|z|\le1$. Then
$$(1-z)P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^na_jz^{n-j}-\sum_{j=0}^na_jz^{n+1-j}=a_n-Q(z),\qquad Q(z)=a_0z^{n+1}+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(a_{j+1}-a_j)z^{n-j}.$$
(Collect the coefficient of $z^{n-j}$: it is $a_j-a_{j+1}$ for $0\le j\le n-1$, $a_n$ for $j=n$, and $-a_0$ for $z^{n+1}$.)

All coefficients $a_0$, $a_{j+1}-a_j$ of $Q$ are positive, and $|z|\le1$, so
$$|Q(z)|\le a_0+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(a_{j+1}-a_j)=a_n .\tag{1}$$

**When can $P(z)=0$?** Then $(1-z)P(z)=0$, so $Q(z)=a_n$ and equality holds in (1). Equality in (1) forces:
- $|z|=1$. If $|z|<1$, then $|a_0z^{n+1}|<a_0$ and (1) is strict.
- All terms of $Q(z)$ have the same argument. In particular $a_0z^{n+1}$ and $(a_1-a_0)z^n$ do, so their quotient $\frac{a_0}{a_1-a_0}z$ is a positive real number, i.e. $z>0$.

Together, $z=1$. But $P(1)=a_0+\dots+a_n>0$. So $P$ has no roots with $|z|\le1$, i.e. every root satisfies $|z|>1$. ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-03.title: Reverse the polynomial
vjimc-1998-cat2-03.body:
Equivalently, show that $R(w)=w^nP(1/w)=a_0+a_1w+\dots+a_nw^n$ has all roots in $|w|<1$. Note $0$ is not a root of $P$, since $P(0)=a_n>0$.

Consider
$$(1-w)R(w)=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^{n}(a_j-a_{j-1})w^j-a_nw^{n+1}.$$
Suppose $|w|\ge1$ and $R(w)=0$. Then $a_nw^{n+1}=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n(a_j-a_{j-1})w^j$. Dividing by $w^{n+1}$ and taking moduli,
$$a_n=\left|\frac{a_0}{w^{n+1}}+\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{a_j-a_{j-1}}{w^{n+1-j}}\right|\le a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n(a_j-a_{j-1})=a_n .$$
Equality requires $|w|=1$ and all terms with the same argument. Then the quotient of consecutive terms, a positive multiple of $w$, is a positive real, so $w=1$. But $R(1)>0$. So all roots $w$ of $R$ satisfy $|w|<1$, and the roots $z=1/w$ of $P$ satisfy $|z|>1$. ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-04m.title: A wild counterexample
vjimc-1998-cat2-04m.body:
**No.** We construct $f$ whose graph meets every non-vertical line above a dense set of abscissas, while $f(0)=0$ and $f(\pm1)=1$.

**Ingredients.**
- Let $\Lambda=\mathbb R^2$ be the set of non-vertical lines $v=\alpha u+\beta$, identified with their coefficients $(\alpha,\beta)$.
- The cosets $r+\mathbb Q$ of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$ are pairwise disjoint, and each is dense in $\mathbb R$. There are continuum many of them (each is countable and they cover $\mathbb R$), and also continuum many cosets other than $\mathbb Q$ itself. $\Lambda$ also has the cardinality of the continuum. So there is a surjection $C\mapsto\lambda_C=(\alpha_C,\beta_C)$ from the set of cosets $C\ne\mathbb Q$ onto $\Lambda$.

**Definition of $f$.**
$$f(u)=\begin{cases}\alpha_Cu+\beta_C,& u\in C,\ C\ne\mathbb Q\text{ a coset (i.e. }u\notin\mathbb Q),\\ |u|,& u\in\{-1,0,1\},\\ 0,& u\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{-1,0,1\}.\end{cases}$$

**The property holds.** Let $x,y\in\mathbb R$. If $x=y$ any $t$ works. If $x\ne y$, let $v=\alpha u+\beta$ be the line through $(x,f(x))$ and $(y,f(y))$. Choose a coset $C\ne\mathbb Q$ with $\lambda_C=(\alpha,\beta)$. Since $C$ is dense, there is $w\in C$ strictly between $x$ and $y$; write $w=tx+(1-t)y$ with $0<t<1$. Then $f(w)=\alpha w+\beta$, and because $u\mapsto\alpha u+\beta$ is affine and passes through $(x,f(x))$ and $(y,f(y))$,
$$f(tx+(1-t)y)=\alpha(tx+(1-t)y)+\beta=t(\alpha x+\beta)+(1-t)(\alpha y+\beta)=tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).$$

**The midpoint property fails.** For $x=-1$, $y=1$: $f(0)=0$, but $\frac{f(-1)+f(1)}2=1$.

**Answer: No.** ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-04m.title: Remark: continuous functions with the property are affine
vjimc-1998-cat2-04m.body:
The counterexample has to be wild. **If $f$ is continuous and has the property, then $f$ is affine** (so the midpoint identity holds).

*Proof.* Let $x<y$, let $\ell$ be the affine function with $\ell(x)=f(x)$, $\ell(y)=f(y)$, and put $h=f-\ell$. Then $h$ is continuous on $[x,y]$ and $h(x)=h(y)=0$. Suppose $h(x_0)\ne0$ for some $x_0\in(x,y)$. Let
$$a=\sup\{u\in[x,x_0]:h(u)=0\},\qquad b=\inf\{u\in[x_0,y]:h(u)=0\}.$$
By continuity $h(a)=h(b)=0$, $a<x_0<b$, and $h\ne0$ on $(a,b)$. Apply the property to the pair $a,b$: there is $t\in(0,1)$ such that $w=ta+(1-t)b\in(a,b)$ satisfies
$$f(w)=tf(a)+(1-t)f(b)=t\ell(a)+(1-t)\ell(b)=\ell(w),$$
i.e. $h(w)=0$, a contradiction. So $f=\ell$ on $[x,y]$. Since $x<y$ were arbitrary, $f$ is affine on $\mathbb R$.

So any counterexample must be discontinuous; the one in the first approach uses a surjection from the cosets of $\mathbb Q$ onto $\mathbb R^2$. ∎

vjimc-1998-cat2-04i.title: Finite automata (Büchi's method)
vjimc-1998-cat2-04i.body:
**Preparation.** Rename bound variables so that distinct quantifiers bind distinct variables. Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be all variables of the formula; every subformula $\varphi$ then defines a relation $R_\varphi\subseteq\mathbb N^n$ (the tuples satisfying it, with variables not free in $\varphi$ ignored). Replace $\forall x\,\varphi$ by $\neg\exists x\,\neg\varphi$ and $\to,\leftrightarrow$ by $\neg,\wedge,\vee$.

**Encoding.** Over the alphabet $\Sigma_n=\{0,1\}^n$ (columns of $n$ bits), a word $w=c_0c_1\dots c_{m-1}$ encodes the tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ with $a_i=\sum_{r}c_r[i]\,2^r$. Row $i$ is the binary expansion of $a_i$, least significant bit first, possibly with trailing zeros. Every word encodes exactly one tuple (the empty word encodes $(0,\dots,0)$), and every tuple has encodings of every length $\ge$ its bit-length. For $R\subseteq\mathbb N^n$ let $\mathcal L(R)$ be the set of *all* encodings of tuples in $R$.

**Claim.** For every subformula $\varphi$ we can effectively construct a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) $A_\varphi$ with $L(A_\varphi)=\mathcal L(R_\varphi)$.

*Atomic formulas* $\mathrm{Plus}(x_i,x_j,x_l)$ (indices may coincide). The DFA has states $\{0,1\}$ (the carry) plus a rejecting sink, with start and only accepting state $0$. Reading a column $c$ in state $\gamma$, let $s=c[i]+c[j]+\gamma$. If $s\equiv c[l]\pmod 2$, go to state $\lfloor s/2\rfloor$; otherwise go to the sink. This checks the school addition algorithm bit by bit. A word is accepted iff $a_i+a_j=a_l$, since a final carry $0$ means no overflow beyond the word length. Trailing zero columns keep state $0$, so all encodings are treated alike.

*Negation.* Every word encodes some tuple, so $\mathcal L(\mathbb N^n\setminus R)=\Sigma_n^*\setminus\mathcal L(R)$. Swap accepting and non-accepting states of the DFA.

*Conjunction / disjunction.* $\mathcal L(R\cap S)=\mathcal L(R)\cap\mathcal L(S)$, and likewise for $\cup$. Use the product automaton.

*Existential quantifier* $\exists x_i\,\varphi$. Let $R'=\{\mathbf a:\exists b\ \mathbf a[i\mapsto b]\in R_\varphi\}$. From $A=A_\varphi$ build a nondeterministic automaton $A'$. On reading a column $c$, it may move like $A$ on $c$ with bit $i$ replaced by $0$ or by $1$ (it guesses the $i$-th row). Its accepting states are the states $q$ of $A$ from which some accepting state is reachable by reading columns that are $0$ except possibly in row $i$. This set is computable by graph search, and it accounts for $b$ having more bits than the input word.
- If $\mathbf a\in R'$ with witness $b$ and $w$ encodes $\mathbf a$, pad: the guessed run on $w$ uses the bits of $b$, and the remaining bits of $b$ are read afterwards in the zero-columns phase. So $A'$ accepts $w$.
- Conversely, an accepting run of $A'$ yields a word accepted by $A$ that encodes $\mathbf a[i\mapsto b]$ for some $b$.

Hence $L(A')=\mathcal L(R')$. The subset construction turns $A'$ into a DFA.

**Deciding truth.** For the closed input formula $\varphi$, $R_\varphi$ is either all of $\mathbb N^n$ (if $\varphi$ is true) or empty (if false). So $\varphi$ is true iff $A_\varphi$ accepts the empty word, i.e. iff its start state is accepting.

All steps are effective, so this is an algorithm deciding the truth of closed formulas of $L$ in $(\mathbb N,+)$ (Presburger arithmetic without constants and order, which are definable anyway). ∎
